Family business includes a campus with about 150 rental units. I did an initial tear-down/shoring up of the backoffice/management portion of the IT when we took over the property. The office complex has a maze with a tonne of extra wiring/spools/dead-ends just stuffed up on top of the drop ceiling tiles. We had a telco contractor come and build a new patch panel for the telco and install new rack for the Mitel PBX. Another IT contractor came in and setup a mini-rack with a patch panel for me where we concentrated new and old wire runs to get all of our office equipment setup. I only had a week so it was pretty half-assed, but this will be a months long project doing it "right" - with a lot of interference in operations during the corrections.

Anyway I just came back to the site and found that the campus-side Open-Mesh network of 60+ nodes was down to about half the nodes functioning. Tenants of the units have been stealing and disconnecting the units. I also found a half dozen dead switches, and a half dozen 20 year old Netgear 10-BaseT hubs. I have been going around discarding the 10-BaseT hubs and aggregating the good 10/100 switches that remained [but which aren't trustworthy, as they are also 15 year old off-brand hardware whose members include all the dead units]. In one chaseway I found 3 network switches hanging by their power cords and the loom of cat-5 cables.

For every inch I gained in getting more Open-mesh nodes online, I would lose a few. About 3 days in - a new problem occurred, nobody could get DHCP leases. So I re-configured our back-office to completely segregate the campus network from the office network [why the IT people we've had maintaining and improving the system in the last year or so since we took over didn't do that I can't explain]

So now our clusterclick of a network is properly segregated and the office is stable. So I dove back into the various chaseways and caches of network hardware stuffed into nooks and crannies and identified two switches with the wrong power supplies, replaced those, and had smooth sailing on the network.

For about 15 hours.

At this point I have made a functional map of the site and am at the point where I can start to have maintenance crew chase the backbone wiring so I can make a good layout drawing and get some cables labeled. I was considering mushroom packets/bad switch or maybe a network loop, so I started doing some Wireshark analysis and then started Zenmapping portions of the network and I found our new problem -

A fairly new [relative to the age of the site] router somewhere. When we acquired the property they were paying a few hundred dollars a month to a company called "Liveport" to "manage" their open-mesh network. This is a service that Cloudtrax replaces, and it comes free with open-mesh hardware. It was a no brainer and the property Manager had been instructed to get rid of Liveport and use Cloudtrax. Liveport never came and picked up their hardware - and in the course of replacing bad switches I have brought one of their edge routers back to life and it is mad at us.

And I can't find it. A problem for tomorrow I suppose.
